meters.label: Transfers executed by the forged request

frames.narration: The user logs in to bank.example. The bank sets a session cookie, which the browser will attach to every later request to bank.example.
In another tab the user opens evil.example. Its page contains a hidden form that points at the bank's transfer endpoint and submits itself.
The browser sends the form to bank.example. Without protection it attaches the bank's cookie, because the destination is the bank, no matter which site started the request.
The bank sees a valid session and does the transfer. The user never clicked anything on the bank's site. This is cross-site request forgery.
Defence 1: the cookie is marked SameSite=Lax. Now the browser withholds it from this cross-site POST, so the bank receives an unauthenticated request and refuses it.

Defence 2: the bank also requires a secret CSRF token that it put in its own pages. evil.example cannot read the bank's pages, so it cannot supply the token, and the request is rejected even if a cookie were sent.

CORS is a different rule. The same-origin policy stops evil.example's scripts from reading the bank's responses. Only if the bank sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin for evil.example can they read them, so never allow origins you do not trust.
